implementation_notes: C++20 designated initializers deliver the named-parameter idiom directly: an aggregate `struct ServerOptions` whose members all carry default member initializers is filled at the call site (`server.run({ .port = 9000, .tls = true })`) and passed by value; unset members keep their defaults, adding a member never reorders existing call sites, and the compiler enforces declaration order instead of silently mixing arguments up. Before C++20 the same contract is expressed with named-parameter function objects (fmt-style, C++11) or Boost.Parameter keyword tags (C++03, library); hand-written constructor overload sets for each combination are what this pattern replaces.
pitfalls: Designators must follow member declaration order and cannot be mixed with positional initializers; reordering members is a source-breaking change, so treat the member order as public API (sorting members alphabetically is a common guard).
Designated initializers cannot be forwarded (`emplace_back(.port = 9000)` is ill-formed); wrap them in the options type when passing through templates or containers.

A designated call relies on default member initializers: a field without one is value-initialized to zero instead of taking a meaningful default, so every option member needs `= value` in the declaration.
Passing the options struct by value copies it on every call; make it small or pass by const reference, and do not store a pointer to a caller's temporary.

variants.name: Named-parameter function objects (fmt-style)
variants.implementation_notes: Where order-independence, composition or pre-C++20 toolchains matter, each option becomes a small function object that knows how to apply itself to the configuration or stream: fmt's text-style values (`fmt::print(fmt::fg(fmt::color::red), ...)`) and hand-rolled `port(9000)` / `timeout(30s)` factories passed to a variadic constructor are the same idea. It composes well (options can be stored and combined) and lifts the declaration-order restriction, at the cost of one type or factory per option and no way to inspect the assembled configuration as an aggregate.
pitfalls: Every option needs its own type or factory plus deduction guides for templates, so the option set is more code than one struct.
Ordering is application order and the last writer wins unless the applier checks conflicts; two options setting the same field cannot be detected by the compiler.
Template/deduction mistakes surface as long errors far from the call site, so option factories need tight constraints (concepts).

variants.name: Boost.Parameter keyword tags (library, pre-C++11)
variants.implementation_notes: Boost.Parameter implements named function and template parameters with keyword tag objects and `parameter::parameters` packing, so an API can accept `(port = 9000, timeout = 5)` in any order with defaults declared per keyword, and it remains the only mechanism that names *template* parameters. It is heavyweight - macros over template metaprogramming, with compile-time cost and error messages that point into the preprocessor - so it is worth using only for existing Boost-based code bases or named template parameters.
variants.code_sketch:
BOOST_PARAMETER_NAME(port)
BOOST_PARAMETER_NAME(timeout)

BOOST_PARAMETER_FUNCTION(
    (Server), make_server, tag,
    (required (host, (std::string)))
    (optional (port, int, 8080) (timeout, int, 30)))

// auto s = make_server((port = 9000), (timeout = 5));
pitfalls: The macros hide the real signature, so compiler errors point into the preprocessor expansion rather than the option.
Header-only metaprogramming: compile times and error complexity grow quickly with each keyword.
It names parameters, not values: the configuration is still a runtime argument, so it does not replace compile-time configuration (constexpr, templates).
